summary.text: For arbitrary \(N\), take \(n=(N+6)!\) and a witnessing decomposition, writing \(p=6x-1\) and \(r=6y+1\), so that \(p+r=6n\), \(p\) is Sophie Germain, and \(r-2,r\) are twin primes. If \(p\le N\), then \(p\mid 6n\) and hence \(p\mid r\) with \(p<r\), while if \(r-2\le N\), then \(r\mid 6n\) and hence \(r\mid p\) with \(r<p\); each contradicts primality, proving both families are unbounded and therefore infinite.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ and }2p+1\text{ are prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
\mathcal T=\{t\in\mathbb N:t\text{ and }t+2\text{ are prime}\}
\]
be the set of smaller members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(A227923(n)\) counts the integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\) such that, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Indeed, its defining sum over \(1\le x<n\) has summand \(1\) exactly when these four primality conditions hold, and summand \(0\) otherwise.

Assume that
\[
A227923(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>1.
\]
We first record the immediate consequence that will be used twice. For every \(n>1\), there are integers \(x,y\ge 1\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\]
and
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\tag{1}
\]
are all prime. To see this, the finite defining sum for \(A227923(n)\) is positive, so at least one of its zero-or-one summands must be \(1\). Its index \(x\) satisfies \(1\le x<n\), and hence \(y=n-x\ge1\), giving precisely (1).

We will prove separately that \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) are unbounded. An unbounded subset of \(\mathbb N\) is infinite, since every finite subset of \(\mathbb N\) has a largest element.

## Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

Fix an arbitrary integer \(N\ge0\). Set
\[
K=N+6,
\qquad n=K!,
\qquad S=6K!=6n.
\]
Since \(K\ge6\), we have \(n>1\). Apply the consequence of the hypothesis above to this \(n\). Thus there are positive integers \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\) for which all four numbers in (1) are prime.

Define
\[
p=6x-1,
\qquad q=6y+1.
\]
The number \(p\) is a Sophie Germain prime: it is prime by (1), and
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is also prime by (1). Moreover, since \(x+y=n\),
\[
p+q=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n=S,
\tag{2}
\]
so equivalently \(q=S-p\). The number \(q\) is prime as well.

We claim that \(p>N\). Suppose instead that \(p\le N\). Since \(p\) is prime, \(p\ge2\), and since
\[
p\le N<K=N+6,
\]
the integer \(p\) is one of the positive integers not exceeding \(K\). Consequently \(p\mid K!\), and hence
\[
p\mid S=6K!.
\]
Together with (2), this implies
\[
p\mid S-p=q.
\tag{3}
\]

On the other hand, \(K!\ge K\), and therefore
\[
S=6K!\ge6K=6N+36>2N+4=2(N+2).
\tag{4}
\]
In particular, because \(p\le N\), (4) gives \(S>2p\). Thus
\[
q=S-p>p.
\tag{5}
\]
Equations (3) and (5) say that the prime \(q\) has a divisor \(p\) satisfying \(2\le p<q\), which is impossible: a prime has no positive divisor other than \(1\) and itself. This contradiction proves \(p>N\).

We have therefore shown that for every \(N\) there is a Sophie Germain prime \(p>N\). Hence \(\mathcal S\) is unbounded and thus infinite.

## Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

Again fix an arbitrary integer \(N\ge0\), and make the same choices
\[
K=N+6,
\qquad n=K!,
\qquad S=6K!.
\]
As before, \(n>1\), so the hypothesis supplies positive integers \(x,y\) with \(x+y=n\) such that all four numbers in (1) are prime.

Now define
\[
p=6x-1,
\qquad t=6y-1,
\qquad r=6y+1.
\]
Both \(t\) and \(r\) are prime, and, because \(y\ge1\), ordinary integer arithmetic gives
\[
r=t+2.
\]
Thus \(t\in\mathcal T\): it is the smaller member of the twin-prime pair \((t,t+2)=(6y-1,6y+1)\). Also \(p\) is prime, and
\[
p+r=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=6(x+y)=6n=S.
\tag{6}
\]

We claim that \(t>N\). Suppose to the contrary that \(t\le N\). Since \(r=t+2\), this gives
\[
r\le N+2<K=N+6.
\tag{7}
\]
The number \(r\) is prime, so in particular it is positive. By (7), \(r\le K\), and consequently \(r\mid K!\). Hence
\[
r\mid S=6K!.
\]
Using (6), we obtain
\[
r\mid S-r=p.
\tag{8}
\]

As in (4),
\[
S>2(N+2).
\]
Since \(r\le N+2\), it follows that \(S>2r\), and (6) therefore yields
\[
p=S-r>r.
\tag{9}
\]
But (8) and (9) say that the prime number \(p\) has a divisor \(r\) with \(2\le r<p\), again impossible. Thus the supposition \(t\le N\) was false, and \(t>N\).

For every \(N\), therefore, there is a twin-prime pair whose smaller member \(t\) exceeds \(N\). The set \(\mathcal T\) is unbounded and hence infinite.

We have proved that the assumed positivity of \(A227923(n)\) for every \(n>1\) implies both that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and that there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
